term: "Vector Quantization"

## Simple explanation

Vector quantization replaces a vector with the ID of a nearby representative
vector from a finite collection, called a codebook. Instead of storing every
number precisely, a system can store a compact code.

## Technical explanation

Given a codebook $C=\{c_1,\dots,c_K\}$, nearest-neighbor quantization assigns
$x$ to an index such as $k^*=\arg\min_k d(x,c_k)$. A quantized representation
uses the corresponding code vector $c_{k^*}$. In neural systems, codebooks may
be learned jointly with an encoder and decoder; training commonly needs
careful handling of the non-differentiable assignment.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Quantization can reduce memory and bandwidth in compression, generative
models, and efficient inference. It introduces approximation error and may
create codebook utilization problems, so compression ratio and task quality
should be measured together.

## How it works

Learn a finite codebook from representative vectors, assign each input to a
code, and store or transmit code indices. A decoder looks up code vectors and
reconstructs an approximation. Multi-stage or product quantization can encode
high-dimensional vectors using several smaller codebooks.

## Practical example

A nearest-neighbor index can compress stored embeddings by representing each
vector with compact code indices. Benchmark recall at the intended latency and
memory budget, because quantized retrieval may miss neighbors found by exact
search.

## Common misconceptions

- Vector quantization is not simply rounding every scalar independently; it
  can quantize groups of dimensions jointly.
- A smaller representation does not guarantee faster end-to-end inference if
  decoding, memory access, or hardware support becomes the bottleneck.
